description: Ego-policy swap experiment over scenarios/local/benchmark, run on the bundled local simulator (--backend pygame) instead of CARLA. Each scenario is run twice: once as compiled (the ego driven by its behaviour-tree timeline) and once with the ego's actuation handed to the IDM policy through the --ego-policy entry point. Everything else -- NPC timelines, events, monitors, spawn geometry -- is identical between the two arms, exactly as in benchmark.json.
relationship_to_benchmark_json: These are ports, not the same runs. The four junction .osc files stage their conflicts at the centre junction (80, 80) of the synthesised `grid` town rather than at Town10HD_Opt junctions 189/841/134, so their absolute numbers are not comparable with benchmark.json; the intended OUTCOME is, and that is what expect_collision encodes. The three highway files are closer than that: nothing in them crosses a junction, so every speed and distance is the same number as in the CARLA original and only the road under them changes (`highway` for lane_change and cut_in, `two_lane` for overtake, standing in for Town04 roads 40 and 51). See the header of each .osc for the per-scenario differences.

idm_parameters.note: Library defaults, identical across all seven scenarios, so the arm differs only in the controller and not in per-scenario tuning.

scenarios.name: red_light
scenarios.intent: A vehicle running the crossing red T-bones the ego inside the junction.

scenarios.name: right_turn
scenarios.intent: A vehicle already on the lane the ego turns onto rear-ends it.

scenarios.name: left_turn
scenarios.intent: An oncoming vehicle strikes the ego mid unprotected-left-turn.

scenarios.name: stop_sign
scenarios.intent: The ego negotiates an unsignalised crossing by precedence and nothing is hit.

scenarios.name: lane_change
scenarios.intent: The ego changes into the one neighbouring lane that is occupied, after the vehicle ahead brakes hard.

observed_scripted.note: partners blocker then lead: the side impact knocks the ego back into its own lane, where the braking lead still is

scenarios.name: cut_in
scenarios.intent: A faster vehicle passes the ego, cuts in ~7 m ahead of it and slows; the ego runs into the back of it.

scenarios.name: overtake
scenarios.intent: The ego pulls out past a slow lorry into the oncoming lane and meets an oncoming car head-on.

junction_turn_note: drive() follows waypoint.next()[0], so which way a vehicle goes through a junction is a property of the lane it is on. --junction-turn sets the map-wide preference and the town's lane-pairing rule supplies the per-actor difference: a left turn is connected only from the innermost lane and a right turn only between outermost lanes, so a vehicle on the other lane has no such connector and goes straight. Each scenario's header comment states which actor is on which lane and why.
construct_vocabulary: These scenarios use only constructs the paper documents -- Table 2's capability checklist and Listings 1-3 of the hello_world case study. ram(target:) has been removed: it appears nowhere in the paper, and every adversarial outcome here previously depended on it. The striking vehicle now keeps executing drive() on its own lane at its own declared speed; drive() has no car-following, yielding or collision-avoidance term, so not changing what you are doing IS failing to give way. See PIPELINE_WALKTHROUGH.md, 'Construct provenance'.
impulse_note: Peak impulses are lower than the CARLA benchmark's and lower than this suite's own earlier ram-based runs. ram applied full throttle regardless of the declared speed; without it the declared speed is the actual speed, so left_turn falls from ~19500 to ~5900 and right_turn from ~12400 to ~4300. collision_occurred and the intended partner are unchanged, and those are what expect_collision and intended_partner test.

sweep.design: Latin hypercube over the six IDM parameters, stratified on every axis
sweep.why_not_repeats: The local simulator is deterministic -- fixed step, no physics substepping, no server, stable spawn digest -- so repeating one configuration reproduces it bit for bit. Unlike the CARLA benchmark, where REPEATS samples the simulator's own variability, repeats here carry no information. The only distribution available is over the policy, so that is what is sampled.
sweep.scripted_arm: The scripted arm has no parameters and is therefore a single deterministic run per scenario: a reference point, not a distribution. Its rates have no confidence interval to report.

report_notes: Repeats would be uninformative. The local backend is deterministic: three identical runs of left_turn produced bit-identical first-contact time, peak impulse, distance and event count, and sweep_idm_local.py --check-determinism asserts this before every sweep. The 64 runs per IDM cell are therefore 64 different parameter vectors, drawn from a Latin hypercube over the six IDM parameters, not 64 repeats. The scripted arm has no parameters and is a single deterministic run.

These rates measure fit to the staged timing, not safety. Each scenario was tuned so that the scripted ego arrives at the conflict when the scripted antagonist does. An IDM ego with different acceleration arrives at a different time, so a low intended-conflict rate mostly says the policy does not match the choreography — not that it drives badly. a_max being the strongest predictor in three of four scenarios is exactly this effect.

The NPCs have no driver model. drive() is a waypoint+PID controller that never yields and never brakes for anything. Any ego slower than the scripted one is rear-ended by its own scripted follower — which happens in 64/64 red_light runs and 59/64 left_turn runs. That is a property of the benchmark, not of IDM, and it is the single biggest caveat on these numbers.

stop_sign is the one clean read. It is the only scenario whose pass condition is the absence of a collision, so it does not depend on meeting a scripted antagonist on schedule. IDM fails it in 19 of 64 samples: it has no term for a crossing conflict, so whether it yields to the crosser is incidental — a consequence of car-following on a vehicle that happens to be ahead, not of giving way.

Six comparisons per scenario. The sensitivity tables split 64 samples at each parameter's median, six times per scenario. With that many comparisons an isolated 15-point gap is unremarkable; only a_max in left_turn (+56 points) is large enough that the 95% intervals of the two halves do not overlap.

Instrumentation is excluded. Each scenario places a ground-decal marker at its conflict point as a distance reference. The local simulator reports a contact when a vehicle drives over one but does not deflect the vehicle, mirroring CARLA; the headline metric counts only vehicle-versus-vehicle contacts, and decal contacts are reported separately as n_static_contacts.

Lateral control is shared. IDM is longitudinal only; steering reuses the same pure-pursuit rule as the compiled drive(), so both arms follow the identical route through each junction and the comparison isolates the longitudinal policy.

Geometry is synthesised. These scenarios run at the centre junction of the local grid town, not at Town10HD_Opt junctions 189/841/134. Absolute numbers are not comparable with the CARLA benchmark; the intended outcome per scenario is.
report_reproducing:
# 64-sample IDM parameter sweep + scripted reference (260 runs, ~1 min on 12 cores)
python experiments/sweep_idm_local.py -n 64 --seed 20260818 --jobs 12 --check-determinism
python experiments/make_report.py experiments/results_local_sweep \
    -c experiments/benchmark_local.json -o experiments/report_local/index.html

# single-sample run of both arms, with bird's-eye recordings
./experiments/run_experiments_local.sh

Needs pygame and nothing else: no CARLA, no GPU, no server, and no Python 3.8
constraint. A no-video run takes ~1.8 s. The sweep is reproducible from the seed:
the sampler is seeded and the simulator is deterministic, so the same seed gives
the same 64 parameter vectors and the same 260 results.
